title: The flood (Genesis 7)
hook: the fountains of the deep break open, and God remembers Noah
tomorrow: The dove and the olive leaf

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ark, a box built on dry land, and your line was build anyway. Did you put in one plank on the thing others doubt? Day three hundred forty-four.

Go back to the very first page. Darkness on the face of the deep. Waters everywhere. Then God divides them: a dome to hold the waters above, seas gathered so dry land can appear. Creation, in Genesis, is partly a story of water being given its place. Now, in chapter seven, the story runs that film backwards. The waters come back. Up from below, down from above. The dry land disappears. It's as if the world is being unmade, returned to the deep. And inside a wooden box, floating on all of it, are Noah, his family, and the animals. Today is the flood, and one small word in the middle of it.
screen: `CREATION: WATER GIVEN ITS PLACE.` → `THE FILM RUNS BACKWARDS.` → `A BOX ON THE DEEP.`

segments.voice: Here's how the King James Bible tells it: "the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened." The deep from verse two of the Bible, and the waters above the dome from day two, both let loose at once. Rain for forty days and forty nights. The waters rise over the mountains, and stay for a hundred and fifty days. Two small details are worth knowing. First, the animals. Everyone knows two by two. But chapter seven also tells Noah to take seven pairs of every clean animal, and the birds. Both are in the text. Second, after everyone is inside, there's this: "and the LORD shut him in." Noah doesn't close the door. God does. Then the long, long wait, in the dark, in the noise, with no land anywhere. And at the turn, the first verse of the next chapter: "And God remembered Noah." In Hebrew, zakhar, to remember. It doesn't mean God had forgotten. In the Bible, when God remembers, God acts. Remembering is the hinge. Right after it, a wind passes over the earth, like the Spirit over the waters at the start, and the waters begin to go down. Christians read the flood in different ways: some as a worldwide event, some as a regional flood remembered in a great story, some as a story whose truth is about God and people more than geology. Other ancient peoples told flood stories too. But in all these readings, the turning point is the same three words: God remembered Noah.
screen: `THE FOUNTAINS OF THE DEEP BROKEN UP.` · `TWO BY TWO, AND SEVEN PAIRS.` · `THE LORD SHUT HIM IN.` · `ZAKHAR: TO REMEMBER IS TO ACT.` · then, large: `AND GOD REMEMBERED NOAH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone who's in deep water. Settle, and breathe. Think of a person who's in over their head right now. Grief, illness, debt, a marriage coming apart, a long dark wait with no land in sight. Picture them clearly, wherever they are this evening. Hold them in mind the way the story says God held Noah. Not just a passing thought. Remembering that leads somewhere. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. After the bell, think of one small act that could follow. The bell holds the time.
The flood. The waters of the first page let loose again, the world almost unmade, and in the middle, the turn: God remembered Noah.
Your line: god remembers. Today, turn remembering into one act for the person in deep water: a message, a meal, a visit. Day three hundred forty-four.

screen: `DAY 344 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE DOVE AND THE OLIVE LEAF.`

howItsDone: Many churches pray for those in trouble by name every week, and the first letter of Peter links the flood to baptism, so the story is often read at baptisms and at the Easter Vigil.

notes: The outline places 'God remembers Noah' in Genesis 7; it is actually Genesis 8:1. The script cites 8:1 as 'the first verse of the next chapter'. Keeper/owner may wish to adjust the outline range.
Seven pairs of clean animals and birds (7:2–3) alongside two by two (6:19–20; 7:9, 15). Confirm wording.
Three readings of the flood (worldwide, regional, theological story) given without ranking; 'other ancient peoples told flood stories too' (e.g. Gilgamesh, Atrahasis) left unnamed. Confirm fairness.
Creation-undone reading (waters of 1:2, 1:6–9 released) is a common commentary reading; confirm.
